content.title: About
content.content: Pork egg foo yung is a stir‑fried egg omelette with pieces of pork, vegetables and soy sauce, popular in Chinese‑American cuisine since the late 1960s. The dish is made from beaten eggs, finely diced pork, onion, carrot and sometimes mushrooms, cooked quickly over high heat until golden.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish first appeared on menus of Chinese restaurants in California in 1968 and quickly became a signature item.
The name “foo yung” comes from Cantonese “fu yung”, meaning “omelet”.
It is traditionally served with rice and soy sauce, often accompanied by crispy fried onions.
While the original recipe used pork, many U.S. versions substitute chicken or beef.
In the 1970s the dish entered fast‑food chains, appearing on the menus of several national chains.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Pork and eggs provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and meat supply vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Pork offers heme iron, which helps prevent anemia.

items.title: Vegetable content
items.content: Carrots, onions and occasional broccoli add fiber, vitamin A and antioxidants.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Eggs provide monounsaturated fats and omega‑3 fatty acids that support heart health.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Soy sauce can add a lot of salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: Pork and eggs make the dish relatively high in calories; portion control is advised for weight management.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Egg white is a common allergen; individuals with egg allergy should avoid the dish.

items.title: Food safety
items.content: Undercooked pork may harbor pathogens; ensure the meat is fully cooked.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve pork egg foo yung hot, sliced into pieces, alongside steamed rice or noodles. Drizzle with soy sauce, chili sauce, or sweet‑sour sauce to taste. Garnish with sliced green onions or cilantro for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in a skillet or microwave with a little oil to retain the crisp exterior.
